summary.text: A finite check shows that for every \(1\le d\le2025\), there are distinct primes \(p,q\) with different final digits, \(pq\le150\), and neither dividing \(d\). Since \(d\) is then invertible modulo \(pq\), some \(i<pq\) satisfies \(a+id\equiv0\pmod{pq}\), so one of the first 150 terms has prime divisors ending in different digits.

full_proof.text:
We prove that the asserted arithmetic progression cannot exist.

Call a positive integer admissible if all of its prime divisors have the same final decimal digit. Thus, if an integer has two prime divisors whose residues modulo \(10\) are different, then it is not admissible.

The main ingredient is the following lemma.

**Lemma.** For every integer \(d\) with \(1\le d\le 2025\), there are distinct primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
pq\le 150,\qquad p\not\mid d,\qquad q\not\mid d,
\]
and
\[
p\not\equiv q\pmod {10}.
\]

**Proof of the lemma.** Consider the following fixed list of pairs:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(2,3),(2,5),(2,7),(2,11),(2,13),\\
&(3,5),(3,7),(3,11),(3,17),\\
&(5,7),(5,11),(5,13),\\
&(7,11),(7,13),(11,13).
\end{aligned}
\]
Every entry in this list is a pair of distinct primes. The two members of each pair have different residues modulo \(10\): their last digits can be read directly from the list. For example, the only potentially confusing omissions are explained by the fact that \(3\) and \(13\) have the same last digit, as do \(7\) and \(17\), and neither of those pairs is included.

Also, every product in the displayed list is at most \(150\). Indeed, the largest product occurring is
\[
11\cdot 13=143<150;
\]
the other products are plainly smaller (in particular, the pair involving \(17\) with the largest other member is \((3,17)\), whose product is \(51\)).

We claim that for any \(d\) in the stated range, at least one displayed pair has neither member dividing \(d\). Suppose, to the contrary, that this is false. Then every displayed pair has at least one member that divides \(d\). Equivalently, whenever one member of one of the displayed pairs does not divide \(d\), the other member must divide \(d\).

We now successively show that each of \(2,3,5,7,11\) must divide \(d\).

* If \(2\nmid d\), then the five pairs
  \[
  (2,3),(2,5),(2,7),(2,11),(2,13)
  \]
  force all of \(3,5,7,11,13\) to divide \(d\). These are distinct primes, so their product divides \(d\). But
  \[
  3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=15015>2025,
  \]
  which is impossible for the positive integer \(d\le2025\). Hence \(2\mid d\).

* If \(3\nmid d\), then the pairs
  \[
  (3,5),(3,7),(3,11),(3,17)
  \]
  force \(5,7,11,17\) all to divide \(d\). Therefore
  \[
  5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot17=6545
  \]
  divides \(d\), again contradicting \(d\le2025\). Hence \(3\mid d\).

* If \(5\nmid d\), then the pairs containing \(5\), namely
  \[
  (2,5),(3,5),(5,7),(5,11),(5,13),
  \]
  force \(2,3,7,11,13\) all to divide \(d\). Their product is
  \[
  2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=6006>2025,
  \]
  a contradiction. Hence \(5\mid d\).

* If \(7\nmid d\), then
  \[
  (2,7),(3,7),(5,7),(7,11),(7,13)
  \]
  force \(2,3,5,11,13\) all to divide \(d\). This would make
  \[
  2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11\cdot13=4290>2025
  \]
  divide \(d\), which is impossible. Hence \(7\mid d\).

* Finally, if \(11\nmid d\), then the pairs
  \[
  (2,11),(3,11),(5,11),(7,11),(11,13)
  \]
  force \(2,3,5,7,13\) all to divide \(d\). Their product is
  \[
  2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13=2730>2025,
  \]
  again impossible. Hence \(11\mid d\).

We have proved that \(2,3,5,7,11\) all divide \(d\). Since these are distinct primes, they are pairwise coprime, and hence their product divides \(d\). But
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310>2025,
\]
contradicting \(d\le2025\). This contradiction proves that at least one pair in the displayed list has both members not dividing \(d\). As already checked, that pair consists of distinct primes with different final digits and product at most \(150\). The lemma follows. \(\square\)

We now disprove the conjecture. Suppose, for contradiction, that there are integers \(a,d\) satisfying
\[
a\ge2,\qquad 1\le d\le2025,
\]
such that every one of the 150 numbers
\[
a,
\ a+d,
\ a+2d,
\ldots,
\ a+149d
\]
is admissible.

Apply the lemma to \(d\), and choose the resulting primes \(p,q\). Thus
\[
p\not\mid d,\qquad q\not\mid d,
\]
\(p\) and \(q\) are distinct, \(p\not\equiv q\pmod {10}\), and \(pq\le150\).

Because \(p\) is prime and does not divide \(d\), we have \(\gcd(d,p)=1\). Similarly, \(\gcd(d,q)=1\). Since \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct primes, they are coprime to one another. It follows that
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Consequently, multiplication by \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\). In particular, the congruence
\[
id\equiv -a\pmod {pq}
\]
has a solution modulo \(pq\). Choose its unique representative \(i\) with
\[
0\le i<pq.
\]
Then
\[
a+id\equiv0\pmod {pq},
\]
so
\[
pq\mid a+id.
\]
In particular,
\[
p\mid a+id\qquad\text{and}\qquad q\mid a+id.
\]

Moreover, because \(pq\le150\) and \(i<pq\), we have
\[
0\le i<150.
\]
Thus \(a+id\) is one of the alleged 150 admissible terms. It is positive—in fact \(a+id\ge a\ge2\)—so the divisibilities above show that \(p\) and \(q\) are genuinely prime divisors of this term. But their final decimal digits differ because
\[
p\not\equiv q\pmod {10}.
\]
Therefore the prime divisors of \(a+id\) do not all have the same final decimal digit. Hence \(a+id\) is not admissible, contradicting the assumption that every term with index \(0\le i<150\) is admissible.

This contradiction applies to every possible \(a\ge2\) and every possible common difference \(1\le d\le2025\). Therefore there do not exist integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) for which all 150 terms \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), occur in A381159. Thus the conjectured arithmetic progression does not exist.
